source_description: ​這是關於香港棒球隊的故事，取材自香港棒球隊員提供的事跡，並由他們演回自己。 棒球在香港是一項幾乎不存在的運動，一個嶄新的球場和一位具魅力的新教練，為一群精力充沛的小伙子帶來希望。這隊野球男在球場外的感情生活，穿插在激烈的球賽間，構成了他們與別不同的青春歲月。 從台北隻身而來的“大帥哥”戴教練，邂逅聰明而美麗的離島少女阿平，在得悉妹妹同樣愛上他後，阿平竟因愛妹情切而主動提議三人行。阿聰是港隊的首席投手, 和捕手阿忠是共同進退的拍檔兼好友。比阿聰年少的阿俊有意挑戰先發投手的位置，令阿忠非常不滿。胸襟廣闊的阿聰毫無保留地幫助阿俊練球，此舉不但令阿俊佩服，更吸引了他的女友移情別戀。連番失戀的阿俊對阿聰的好感郤越來越強烈… 兩年一度的“亞洲盃”棒球大賽，從未有過好成績的港隊狀態大勇，連敗強敵，只要在最後一場輕取最弱的斯里闌卡，就可以奪得冠軍，創造歷史。當勝利在望之時…,

source_description: In 1996 South Korean legislative election, two famous big shot politicians collided in Jongno District constituency; Lee Myung-bak and Roh Moo-hyun. This photo, taken at Muak-dong of Jongno District, shows election posters of Lee and Roh in 1996. Though Lee won this election, he had to step down from member of the National Assembly (South Korean legislative) elected in Jongno District, since he was under charges of violating election laws. Left vacancy was filled by Roh in coming by-election. This political event has nationwide popularity in South Korea, as both of them later became the President of South Korea respectively.

source_description: НАГЛЕДНА ТАБЛИЦА ЗА ОБУЧЕНИЕ НА МЛАДИТЬ ВОЙНИЦИ (English: "Visual Chart for the Training of Young Soldiers") Bulgarian military educational poster from the late 1920s, used to train young recruits during the reign of Tsar Boris III (1918–1943); Army of the Tsardom of Bulgaria . Uniforms: Prazdnichna forma ( Празднична форма ): Parade or ceremonial (Dress) uniforms. Stroeva i boina forma ( Строева и бойна форма ): Field (combat) and service uniforms. Central banner: For Distinction in the Turkish War 1877–1878 ( ЗА ОТЛИЧИЕ В ТУРСКАТА ВОЙНА 1877–1878 ГОД. ); refers to the Russo-Turkish War, which led to Bulgaria’s liberation from Ottoman rule. The Samara Flag ( САМАРСКОТО ЗНАМЕ ), famous Bulgarian battle flag from the 1877–1878 war. (Text by AI ) Uncredited artwork. No known copyright restrictions due to its age. The image appears to have been retouched (brightened).

source_description: Official notice, posted by A. Hanciu, the Mayor Paşcani, Romania. Issued shortly after Romania entered the war against the Soviet Union, it announces an antisemitic curfew and warns that Jewish hostages would be shot in the event of behind-the-lines "sabotage" or "terrorism", including acts attributable to non-Jews. The text makes reference to "communist" agitation, and, unusually, to "communist Legionaries". The epithet is apparently oxymoronic: "Legionaries" were the Iron Guard, a fascist and antisemitic movement which had rebelled against the traditionalist far right, and was therefore repressed by the Ion Antonescu government. The poster possibly references a conspiracy theory, according to which some Legionaries were pro-Soviet, differentiating between them and the loyalist ("Codrenist") wing of the Iron Guard. Here, Hanciu cites specific orders from the fascist hierarchy: Ion...

"In consequence of the carriage of letters by travellers in large numbers, infringing the post office monopoly, and causing loss of postal revenue, the authorities created a special postal contraband service. These contraband letters were taxed at double rates of postage, and half of the fees collected thereon was supposed to be given to any informer. The Turkish word for contraband is Katchak, and this special organisation was known as the Katchak Post. At first the tax was denoted by ordinary postage stamps affixed to the letters and obliterated with a hand-stamp showing the word Katchak in a double-lined rectangular frame. source_description: In May and June 1840, British sovereignty was declared over Aotearoa New Zealand by William Hobson and Thomas Bunbury. Signings of te Tiriti o Waitangi continued however, and so did other plans to colonise the country – such as the French settlement in Akaroa. French and German settlers had left France on 20 March 1840 on the Comte de Paris , preceeded by Captain Charles François Lavaud ( www.flickr.com/photos/archivesnz/15776026614 ). Lavaud’s task was to pave the way for the settlement based on a dubious land purchase made in 1838. He arrived in the Bay of Islands on 10 July 1840, and was dismayed to find the British Flag flying and the HMS Britomart at anchor – symbols of the new British status of Aotearoa New Zealand. source_collection: Stamp of NZ Company settlers arriving in Pito-one (Petone), 1840
source_description: On 22 January 1840, the first of the New Zealand Company’s fleet of six immigrant ships, the Aurora , arrived in Pito-one (Petone), marking the founding of the settlement that would become known as Wellington. They had bet William Hobson to Aotearoa New Zealand by seven days; their efforts of self-government would become the cause of some concern to Hobson as he gathered signatures for te Tiriti o Waitangi. This stamp was designed for the 1940 Centennial of New Zealand as a British Colony, and interperets the NZ Company settlers arriving at Pito-one. It was originally produced in colour, but this version comes from a series of Post & Telegraph Department negatives. This record is part of #Waitangi175, celebrating 175 years since the signing of of te Tiriti o Waitangi. You can see other real time tweets on Twitter ( www.twitter.com/ArchivesNZ ), or explore the Waitangi 175 album here on...

source_description: On 18 July 1855, New Zealand's first postage stamps went on sale. The 1 penny, 2 pence and 1 shilling stamps were printed in Britain and featured the famous ‘Chalon Head’ design portraying a full-face likeness of Queen Victoria in her coronation robes. This is a photograph of the original stamp from the 'Former Post and Telegraph/Telecom Museum Holdings' (Series 8106). Also reproduced in the series is a swag of other stamps from the nineteenth and twentieth centuries - a stamp enthusiasts' and graphic designers' dream! Archives New Zealand also holds Internal Affairs correspondence from 1855 dealing with the importation and distribution of the Queen Victoria stamps (see IA1: www.archway.archives.govt.nz/ViewFullItem.do?code=23523603 ). Archives Reference: AAME W5603 8106 Box 148/ 9/12/139 www.archway.archives.govt.nz/ViewFullItem.do?code=20942147 For updates on our On This Day series...

source_description: On January 2 1880, the first excursion train trip from Dunedin to Lake Wakatipu took place. Dunedin was linked to Christchurch by rail in 1878, with a link south to Invercargill completed the following year, and the first railway workshops were opened at Hillside in South Dunedin in 1875. Early plans were for a grand main station on Cumberland Street, but these did not get further than the laying of a foundation. The foundation stone was laid by the Minister of Railways Joseph Ward on June 3, 1904. The Prime Minister Richard Seddon was also present. The station was opened by Ward, by then Prime Minister, in 1906. Construction was kept within budget, and cost £40,000 In its early days the station was the country's busiest, handling up to 100 trains a day, including suburban services to Mosgiel and Port Chalmers, railcars to Palmerston and the Otago Central Railway and other trains to...

source_description: On this day across New Zealand, families have slept off their Christmas and Boxing Day feasts and hit the busy roads for their summer holiday. The exodus to beaches, baches or campgrounds has a long tradition in New Zealand, although some things have indeed changed. In days past it was by train that happy campers made their city escape. As Te Ara notes, in the early 1920s (when New Zealand’s population was only just over 1 million) New Zealand Railways was carrying 28 million passengers a year. Holiday times were hectic: "on Christmas Eve in 1938, 16 express trains (including eight bound for Auckland) swept more than 11,000 travellers out of Wellington in a single day." source_description: On 24 March 1990, the first New Zealand International Carillon Festival (and the first in the Southern Hemisphere) began in Wellington. It ran for a month and showcased the carillon’s continuing contributions to the local soundscape. Depicted in this striking poster for the festival is the centrepiece of the National War Memorial, the 51-metre-high carillon tower, which soars above Pukeahu (Mount Cook). Inside is the carillon itself, one of the largest musical instruments in the world. It is played using a clavier (keyboard) consisting of rows of wooden keys which the carillonist plays with their hands and feet. First built in 1932, the carillon tower has recently been earthquake strengthened as part of the National War Memorial upgrade. More information on the history of the tower, and the carillon instrument can be found at www.mch.govt.nz/pukeahu/park/national-war-memorial/carillon...

These included multiple musical, dance and theatre performances, as well as a fair, a film festival, an art exhibition, a parade, a book week, an ethnic cultural day, a chess tournament, an ice skating championship, a horse show, orienteering, a BMX meet, a skateboarding demonstration, an archery tournament, and even a boomerang workshop. source_description: This poster was created in support of the second conscription referendum put to the Australian people on 20 December 1917 by Prime Minister Hughes. It asked citizens: Are you in favour of the proposal of the Commonwealth Government for reinforcing the Commonwealth Forces overseas?' The referendum was defeated with 1,015,159 in favour and 1,181,747 against. Significantly the poster incorporates a quote by former Prime Minister Andrew Fisher. At the time Fisher was serving as Australia’s High Commissioner in London and opposed Hughes on the issue of conscription.

source_description: Australian Government poster - "Australia: land of Tomorrow". This poster was displayed between 1949 and 1951 in reception rooms and dining halls at various migrant reception centers in Australia. It was placed to introduce and entice newcomers to Australia. The creator of this colourful and light-hearted poster, Joe Greenberg, was told later by a Czech migrant that it had been displayed in all the migrant camps in Europe, and had influenced him to come to Australia.

source_description: Australian Second World War poster. The top half of the poster features a cartoon by Alex Gurney of an Australian soldier having a bright idea. The title for the poster is written into the soldiers' speech bubble and the caricature representing the idea popping out of the soldiers head is a mosquito instead of a light bulb. The poster is designed to encourage people to come up with ideas on saving waste or to think of new inventions for equipment. The lower half of the poster is all text directing people where to send their ideas in each state capital. Alex Gurney was a cartoonist, most famous in the Second World War for his comic strip 'Bluey and Curley', first published in the Melbourne Sun, in February 1941.

source_description: From its conquest by the British in 1839 up to 1937, British Aden was a dependency of India and consequently postage stamps from India were used. Only the postmark (either "Aden", "124" or "B-22") would indicate that the postal item had been posted in Aden. Dedicated stamps for Aden needed to be issued when Aden was separated from India in 1937 to become a Crown Colony ruled from London. Normally, crown colony stamps would bear the effigy of the ruling monarch but when the new stamps were prepared in 1936, the so-called abdication crisis was unfolding. Not quite sure if Edward VIII would still be king when the stamps were printed, the postal authorities played it safe and designed a stamp without any royal portrait, which was issued 1 April 1937. A new regular issue bearing the effigy of George VI was issued in 1939. The Indian rupee continued to be the currency of Aden. In 1951,...

source_description: 5 Centavo overprint on 4 Centavo United States of America Philippine Islands 1935 Agriculture issue (Woman and Carabao statue) postage stamp overprinted under Japanese occupation commemorating the "First Anniversary of the Great East Asia War" Postmark: MANILA *PHILIPPINES* DEC 8 1942 PM (CDS) Base stamp: 4c Agriculture issue of 1935 (yellow green) Overprint in black: "First Anniversary, Greater East Asia War" (in Japanese) with date "12-8-1942" and value "5" (over "4" Centavos) ; Deleting bar at top to obliterate "United States of America" NOTE: Although the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor took place on the morning of Sunday, December 7, 1941, Hawaiian time, as Japan is West of the International Date Line it was Monday there thus making December 8, 1942, the correct date in Asia to observe the first anniversary of the start of the War.
